newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl rejects SPD summit offer of talks on taxes.
newsitem.headline: Kohl rejects SPD summit offer of talks on taxes.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Wednesday rejected an offer of face-to-face talks on tax reform with the leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), but said the talks could resume in a working group of top officials.
The reply amounted to a rebuff to SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine, who sent a letter to Kohl inviting the chancellor to discuss the issues with Lafontaine personally.
Kohls letter said the talks should be resumed as soon as possible but added that the proposals made in Lafontaines letter had all been discussed by the two sides last month.

He also proposed that talks should be restarted in the same group of six officials, including Finance Minister Theo Waigel and SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping, who failed to make progress in the earlier negotiations.
The prospects for any resumption appeared dim when an SPD spokeswoman reacted to Kohls letter saying: Kohl is chickening out.
She did not specify, however, whether the SPD was prepared to resume talks even if Kohl was not present.

The SPD pulled out of the talks two weeks ago in protest at a government plan to cut subsidies to the coal mining industry. Kohl needs the cooperation of the SPD to launch his major tax reform because the SPD have a majority in the upper house and so could block many of the measures.
But since then, it has focused more on setting conditions for the agenda of the talks.
Chief whip Peter Struck confirmed a newspaper report that the SPD wanted a two-point cut in unemployment and pensions insurance contributions from July 1 of this year.

In an apparent change of position, he said the SPD was prepared to raise value added tax as well as petrol tax to compensate for the extra costs to the budget of slashing occupational insurance charges.
But an SPD spokeswoman dismissed the report, in the daily Bild, as pure speculation.
Despite the confusion, the SPD has made clear that it wants a big cut in income tax from the start of 1998 which would benefit ordinary workers and their families and kick-start economic demand.
The SPD position looks to be far away from Waigels plan to cut 30 billion marks in corporate and income taxes by 1999.

Kohls cabinet on Tuesday cleared Waigels 1998 tax bill, which would cut both corporate and commercial income tax rates to a unified 40 percent, as well as knocking two points off the 7.5 percent solidarity income tax surcharge.
The bill, which would lighten the tax burden by 7.5 billion marks, would pave the way for big cuts in the bottom and top rates of income tax, and a further round of corporate tax cuts in 1999.
Coalition parties are expected to introduce the tax bill to parliament this Friday.
